name: MSG/EML File Metadata
location: No fixed location - individual .msg (Outlook drag-and-save, or 'Save As' from a message) and .eml (saved by most other mail clients, and by Outlook when exporting/forwarding as RFC 822) files can appear anywhere on disk: user Documents/Desktop, Downloads folder, email attachments, removable media, or extracted attachments from an OST/PST.
purpose: Individual saved-email files that carry a full self-contained copy of one message, independent of any mailbox store. .msg is Microsoft's OLE/Compound File Binary Format (CFBF) container preserving Outlook-specific MAPI properties; .eml is a plain-text file following the RFC 822/MIME structure used by virtually every other mail client, making it the more portable but MAPI-metadata-poor of the two.
key_fields: MSG: OLE Compound File Binary Format container - each MAPI property (subject, sender, recipients, body, flags, categories, follow-up dates) lives in its own named stream; recipients and attachments each get their own storage, extractable independent of Outlook

MSG: PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS (0x007D) property - the original raw internet headers (including the full Received chain) preserved even though the message is now stored in Outlook's proprietary format
EML: plain-text RFC 822/MIME header block at the top of the file - From, To, Cc, Subject, Date, Message-ID, and the Received header chain, human-readable without any special parser

Received headers (both formats) form a stack, each relay prepending its own line; read bottom-up to trace the hop-by-hop path from originating server to final delivery, per RFC 5321 section 4.4 timestamp/host semantics
Authentication-Results header (EML, and preserved in MSG's transport headers) - SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification outcomes, which are far harder to forge than the From/Reply-To fields themselves

MIME boundary-delimited attachment sections (EML) vs. discrete attachment storages (MSG) - both preserve original attachment filenames and content, independent of whether the parent mailbox still contains the item
Filesystem metadata of the saved file itself (created/modified/accessed timestamps) - reflects when the message was exported to disk, not when it was originally sent/received
normal_baseline: Saved .msg/.eml files correspond to messages the user can explain (an attachment they saved, an email exported for a ticket/case), with filesystem save-timestamps that align with a plausible reason to export that specific message, and internal headers consistent with the claimed sender.
anomalies: A saved .msg/.eml file whose internal Date/Received headers place the original message well before the user account or mailbox existed, or whose Message-ID domain doesn't match any header's claimed sending server - suggesting a fabricated or edited file
Missing or truncated Received header chain on an EML that should have passed through multiple hops, consistent with hand-crafted phishing lures rather than genuine delivered mail

A .msg file's PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS stream absent or empty despite the message showing standard sender/recipient properties, which is atypical for genuinely-delivered mail and can indicate the item was manually constructed in Outlook rather than received
SPF/DKIM/DMARC results in Authentication-Results showing fail/none on a message purporting to be from an internal or trusted domain

Saved-file location or naming inconsistent with normal user workflow (e.g., staged in a temp directory with sequential generic names), suggesting bulk export for exfiltration rather than individual message handling

Discrepancy between the file's filesystem timestamps and the internal message Date header far exceeding what a simple save/forward would produce, suggesting the file was copied from another system or backdated
parsing_tools: MFCMAPI (Microsoft, open-source - browses MSG MAPI properties, converts MSG to/from EML)
extract-msg (open-source Python library for reading MSG/CFBF structure and MAPI properties)
Any text editor (EML is plain text; headers are human-readable without a parser)
anti_forensic_notes: Because EML is plain text and MSG headers are user-editable through MAPI property editors like MFCMAPI, both formats can be hand-crafted or altered to fabricate a convincing-looking message - unlike a message still resident in a live mailbox store or mail server log, a standalone saved file has no independent chain of custody proving it was actually delivered. Cross-referencing the file's internal Received chain and Message-ID against the corresponding OST/PST store or mail server logs (where available) is the primary way to validate authenticity; absence of any corroborating server-side record for a claimed-received message is itself a red flag.
